newsitem.title: PERU: Peru asks for patience in three-month hostage saga.
newsitem.headline: Peru asks for patience in three-month hostage saga.

text.p: The government called on Monday for patience in the three-month standoff with Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home.
Government negotiator Domingo Palermo told reporters he did not know when Latin America's longest hostage siege would end.
"These matters unfortunately take an indeterminate amount of time," he said. "Nobody can fix a time limit for such a delicate subject."

As the siege passed its 90-day milestone, Peruvians vented their frustration with the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels, banging pots, ringing church bells and sounding car horns to demand the hostages be freed.
Mediators shuttled between meetings with both sides in effort to unblock stalled peace talks. But after four hours of discussions they could not offer the prospect of fresh negotiations.
The hostages' relatives who were without their loved ones at Christmas and New Year's "should have a little bit of patience," Palermo said.
A leading pollster said more than half of Peruvians believed the crisis would take at least one month more to resolve.
In a short speech, President Alberto Fujimori also had little to offer his country beyond lamenting the captives' plight as a "terrible situation."
Earlier, families of the hostages holed up in the mansion staged a day of solidarity, including a noisy nationwide demonstration at midday.
In a chaotic cacophany outside the residence, car owners set off their alarms, neighbours came out to bang pots, pans and bottles, and demonstrators blew whistles and chanted.
In the surrounding San Isidro neighbourhood -- as throughout Peru -- churches held special masses and rang bells in a sign of support for the captives.
In Lima, motorists sounded horns, and legislators came out of Congress to hold a minute's silence in a nearby square before applauding and shouting for the hostages' freedom.
Some of the hostages responded by raising hands to a window sandwiched between a rebel flag and a banner railing against Fujimori. One of them waved a white handkerchief.
An open letter from the families described the time since the MRTA takeover of the diplomatic compound as "three months of agony and suffering."

The captives -- diplomats, security chiefs, government ministers, judges and businessmen -- are mainly middle-aged and increasingly ailing, intelligence and medical reports said. Stress, gum diseases and skin ailments are common.
The government negotiator pointedly did not mention Bolivian ambassador Jorge Gumucio, who argued with a rebel last week and is reportedly showing signs of emotional breakdown.
His wife took part in the demonstration outside the residence on Monday. "I hope that inside they all feel that we are with them, that we love them," Beatriz de Gumucio said.

In a sign of Tokyo's growing impatience at the length of the crisis, Japan's Vice Foreign Minister Masahiko Komura was due to land in Peru early on Tuesday on the first leg of a three-nation tour. Komura also was expected to visit Cuba and the Dominican Republic to seek cooperation in arranging asylum for the rebels should they agree to leave Peru.

More than 500 hostages were taken on Dec. 17, 1996, when about 20 jungle-trained rebels blew a hole in the residence's outer wall and swarmed into the building in a fierce shootout. But the MRTA gradually released most of its prisoners, keeping those it considered most valuable as bargaining chips to demand the freedom of some 400 jailed comrades.
